claims.text: Conventionally cast CoCrFeNiTi has low hardness because of coarse grains and porosity.
Approximately 6 hours of high-energy ball milling produces sufficient lattice strain in CoCrFeNiTi.
Approximately 6 hours of high-energy ball milling sufficiently refines the grains of CoCrFeNiTi.
Milling-induced lattice strain and grain refinement lower the energy barrier for an FCC/BCC solid-solution transition.
Spark plasma sintering at 1000°C densifies the milled CoCrFeNiTi powder.
SPS at 1000°C stabilizes an FCC phase in CoCrFeNiTi.
SPS at 1000°C avoids excessive Ti-driven HCP precipitation.
VEC and atomic-radius mismatch govern the relevant FCC/BCC phase stability window in CoCrFeNiTi.
Six hours of milling generates high-density dislocation networks and a nanocrystalline grain size below 100 nm.
Milling-induced defects alter stacking-fault energy and the phase-stability landscape.
Titanium typically drives HCP formation in this quinary alloy.
The VEC of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi is near an FCC stability threshold.
The rapid SPS thermal cycle at 1000°C prevents formation of Ti-rich HCP or Laves phases.
The proposed process will produce a bulk alloy with less than 2% porosity.
The processed alloy will have a single-phase or dual-phase FCC/BCC microstructure.
The processed alloy will exhibit Vickers hardness above 400 HV and more than 50% above the cast baseline.
Hardness will arise primarily from grain-boundary strengthening rather than precipitation hardening.
Sintering above 1100°C causes grain growth and precipitation of Ti-rich HCP or Laves phases.
Milling beyond 10 hours causes excessive carbide or oxide contamination that degrades mechanical properties.
Optimal milling times vary by alloy composition, with 40 hours used for NbMoTaWVTi and an asserted 10 hours for Al-Nb-Ta-Ti-V-based material.

contradictions.description: The boundary says temperatures above 1100°C precipitate Laves phases, whereas the baseline characterizes temperatures above 1200°C as causing Laves-phase decomposition. These descriptions imply opposing Laves-phase trends in overlapping temperature ranges without explaining a sequential precipitation/decomposition process.

The hypothesis describes a lowered thermodynamic energy barrier, while the mechanism describes a lowered activation energy. A thermodynamic free-energy difference and a kinetic activation barrier are distinct quantities, so the proposed controlling barrier is not consistently defined.
